panels.rationale: Fused 18FDG PET/CT transaxial image of a real patient showing a hyperfixating metastasis in the left cerebellum from NSCLC, directly captioned and discussed in-text; supports cerebellar metastasis (brain metastases). Single-panel figure with crosshair/orientation annotations.
panels.attribution_text: Palumbo et al. SPECT and PET serve as molecular imaging techniques and in vivo biomarkers for brain metastases.. International journal of molecular sciences 2014. doi:10.3390/ijms15069878. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: 2-Deoxy-[18F]fluoro-d-glucose(18FDG), positron emission tomography(PET)/computerized tomography (CT) image (transaxial section) of a patient with a metastasis in the left cerebellum deriving from non-small-cell-lung cancer (NSCLC). The metastasis appears as an area of hyperfixation of 18FDG in the context of normal cerebellar parenchyma with homogeneous and symmetrical radiopharmaceutical distribution.
in_text_mentions: The uptake mechanism of 18FDG in tumour cells depends on the increased number of functional glucose transporters and glycolytic enzymes [5]. 18FDG is physiologically and homogeneously distributed in both cerebral and cerebellar hemispheres (glucose avid) and brain tumours are visualized as lesions with higher or lower radiopharmaceutical uptake comparing with normal brain parenchyma [3]. An example of a cerebellar metastasis deriving from lung tumour imaged by 18FDG PET/CT is reported in Figure 1.

findings.label: Leptomeningeal enhancement
findings.evidence: Diffuse nodular leptomeningeal enhancement is seen over the left cerebellar surface on (A) post-contrast 3D T1 FSPGR

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Post-contrast 3D T1 FSPGR MRI of a 68-year-old with lung adenocarcinoma showing diffuse nodular leptomeningeal enhancement over the left cerebellar surface, i.e. leptomeningeal carcinomatosis — a specific manifestation of brain metastases captured in the provided vocabulary. [raw subtype: leptomeningeal] B: Post-contrast 3D T1 CUBE MRI of the same patient demonstrating more conspicuous diffuse nodular leptomeningeal enhancement over the left cerebellar surface, confirming leptomeningeal carcinomatosis as a manifestation of brain metastases. [raw subtype: leptomeningeal]
panels.attribution_text: Tong et al. Advanced Imaging of Brain Metastases: From Augmenting Visualization and Improving Diagnosis to Evaluating Treatment Response.. Frontiers in neurology 2020. doi:10.3389/fneur.2020.00270. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: 68-years-old patient with primary lung adenocarcinoma and leptomeningeal carcinomatosis. Diffuse nodular leptomeningeal enhancement is seen over the left cerebellar surface on (A) post-contrast 3D T1 FSPGR and (B) post-contrast 3D T1 CUBE, compatible with leptomeningeal carcinomatosis. Conspicuity of enhancement is increased in (B) compared to (A).
in_text_mentions: s. Specifically, the vasculature appears bright on post-contrast 3D T1 FSPGR but appears dark (“black blood”) on post-contrast 3D T1 FSE. As a result of the “bright blood” appearance on post-contrast FSPGR, it can sometimes be difficult to distinguish enhancing parenchymal metastases or leptomeningeal carcinomatosis (Figure 1) from background vascular enhancement (12). On the contrary, post-contrast FSE provides inherent background vascular suppression, yielding a higher contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) of lesions, making enhancing parenchymal, and leptomeningeal metastases more conspicuous (13).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Real patient axial and coronal post-contrast T1 MRI of melanoma brain metastases with ependymal (leptomeningeal) metastatic enhancement along the lateral ventricles, a recognized imaging pattern of leptomeningeal metastasis from brain-metastatic disease; arrows and asterisk annotations present. B: Real patient axial and sagittal post-contrast T1 MRI showing the classical linear leptomeningeal metastatic pattern along the trigeminal nerves and cerebellar surface ('sugarcoating') in lung cancer brain metastases; arrowheads/arrows annotations present. C: Real patient axial post-contrast T1 MRI showing the nodular subtype of leptomeningeal metastasis (multiple small superficial enhancing nodules) in lung cancer brain metastases; arrows annotation present.

panels.figure_caption: Different appearances of LM by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). (A) Patient with melanoma brain metastases. Axial (left) and coronal (right) T1 post contrast images demonstrate ependymal metastases along the lateral ventricles (arrows). There are also post-surgical changes related to the prior resection of a parietal parenchymal metastasis (asterisk). (B) Patient with lung cancer brain metastases. Axial (left) and sagittal (right) T1 post contrast images demonstrate linear, “classical”, leptomeningeal metastases along the trigeminal nerves (arrowheads) and “sugarcoating” the cerebellum (arrows). (C) Patient with lung cancer brain metastases. Axial T1 post contrast images demonstrate multiple small, superficially-located lesions, representing nodular leptomeningeal metastases
in_text_mentions: LM can display a diverse range of features by MRI. The enhancement pattern can be nodular, linear, or curvilinear, as well as focal or diffuse [65] (Figure 3). panels.figure_caption: MRI of the brain performed subsequently to 18F-FDG-PET/CT. (A) Coronal and transaxial T2 images; (B) Sagittal and transaxial T1 TSE images. The study showed multiple metastatic lesions, widespread throughout the brain, hypointense on T2 and hyperintense on T1 images.Moreover, a large edema in the white matter of the right cerebral hemisphere and a lesion in the frontal bone infiltrating the meninx were observed. Therefore, due to extensive brain metastases [9,10,11,12] and worsening of treatment adverse effects [4], immunotherapy was discontinued and the patient was subjected to the best supportive care until his conditions progressively worsened to death after a few months.

in_text_mentions: A 41-year-old man was referred to our neurosurgical department after a one-month history of left side partial sensitive seizures and a recent onset of left side hemiparesis. His medical history was unremarkable. A post-contrast computed tomography (CT) scan showed multiple brain lesions: right side parietal (19 mm), left side rolandic (14 mm), and two subcentimetric lesions in the right temporal lobe. On magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), these lesions appeared as partially necrotic and hemorrhagic, with perilesional oedema and enhancement after gadolinium (Figures 1A-1B).

panels.attribution_text: Lao et al. Delayed multiple hemorrhagic brain metastases from atrial myxoma: a case report and literature review.. Frontiers in neuroscience 2026. doi:10.3389/fnins.2026.1859294. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Brain CT and MRI findings. Non-contrast CT images show hemorrhagic space-occupying lesions in the cerebellar vermis (a) and left occipital lobe (b). Axial T1-weighted images show the corresponding lesions in the cerebellar vermis (c) and left occipital lobe (d). Axial T2-weighted images demonstrate heterogeneous signal intensity and perilesional edema in the cerebellar vermis (e) and left occipital lobe (f). Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images show heterogeneous enhancement of the cerebellar vermis lesion (g) and left occipital lesion (h). Red arrows indicate representative lesions. Preoperative brain CTA, provided in Supplementary Image 1, showed no suspicious intracranial aneurysm.
in_text_mentions: al edema, most prominently in the cerebellar vermis and left occipital lobe (approximately 18 mm × 12 mm), together with additional multifocal hemorrhagic lesions in both cerebral hemispheres and the cerebellum. Multiple chronic lacunar infarctions were also present. Preoperative brain CTA showed no suspicious intracranial aneurysm (Supplementary Image 1). This supratentorial and infratentorial distribution raised concern for hemorrhagic malignant metastases or vascular lesions, but the prior history of atrial myxoma made myxoma-related brain metastases an important alternative (Figures 2a–h).

in_text_mentions: In April 2014, a 62-year-old male, non-smoker came to our attention with a sudden weakness, mainly in right upper limb. A total body computed tomography (CT) scan showed a lesion of 4.5 cm in diameter in the right upper lobe of the lung with an omolateral mediastinal lymphadenopathy and multiple, large and diffuse brain lesions (Figure 1A and Figure 2). After diagnostic bronchoscopy he was histologically diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.

panels.rationale: Axial post-gadolinium T1-weighted MRI of the brain showing an intensely and heterogeneously enhancing nodular lesion with a small non-enhancing component and surrounding vasogenic edema (green outline), consistent with a brain metastasis in a case report of brain metastases from Merkel cell carcinoma. The homogeneous enhancing nodule key does not fit the heterogeneous enhancement, so this is proposed as a free-text finding.
panels.attribution_text: Rebelo et al. Challenges in Managing Brain Metastases From Merkel Cell Carcinoma in an Immunosuppressed Patient: A Case Report.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.98538. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: Post-gadolinium T1-weighted MRI image showing a heterogeneous enhancement. Post-gadolinium T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) image showing intense, nodular, and somewhat heterogeneous enhancement, particularly in the central part of the lesion, with a small non-enhancing area. The lesion (red circle) and the surrounding vasogenic edema (green circle) are indicated.
in_text_mentions: After gadolinium administration, there was intense, nodular, and somewhat heterogeneous enhancement, particularly in the central part of the lesion, with a small non-enhancing area. The lesion measured 34 × 36 × 34 mm on MRI, compared with 26 × 27 mm on the prior CT scan, reflecting improved delineation on MRI (Figure 4).

A: Immunohistochemistry of a melanoma patient's brain and lung metastases (Melan A, ERK, p-ERK at 40x) documents metastatic tumor cells in brain tissue, a specific manifestation of brain metastases. Panel is part of a compound figure; no separate storage. B: Higher magnification (200x) view of the same brain and lung melanoma metastases stained for Melan A, ERK and p-ERK, showing metastatic tumor deposits in brain tissue. C: Immunohistochemical staining (Melan A, AKT, p-AKT at 40x) of brain and lung melanoma metastases; the cerebral metastasis shows strong p-AKT positivity, a specific manifestation of metastatic melanoma in brain. D: 200x immunohistochemistry of brain and lung melanoma metastases (Melan A, AKT, p-AKT), demonstrating metastatic tumor cells in brain with activated AKT staining. panels.attribution_text: Niessner et al. Targeting hyperactivation of the AKT survival pathway to overcome therapy resistance of melanoma brain metastases.. Cancer medicine 2013. doi:10.1002/cam4.50. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: (A–E) Brain and lung metastases from a melanoma patient were stained to detect the melanocytic marker Melan A, total and activated ERK (p-ERK), total and activated AKT (p-AKT), and PTEN; 40×: 40-fold magnification, 200×: 200-fold magnification. (F) Brain metastasis from a melanoma patient was stained for p-AKT (red) and HMB-45 (brown) to detect melanoma cells, 200×: 200-fold magnification. The insert shows colocalization of p-AKT (red) with HMB-45 (brown), 630-fold magnification. (G) Brain metastasis from a melanoma patient was stained for p-AKT (red) and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) (brown) to detect glial cells, 200×: 200-fold magnification. GFAP does not colocalize with p-AKT. (H) Brain metastasis from a melanoma patient was stained for p-AKT (red) and CD14 (brown) to detect monocytes/macrophages, 200×: 200-fold magnification. CD14 does not colocalize with p-AKT.

panels.attribution_text: Lao et al. Delayed multiple hemorrhagic brain metastases from atrial myxoma: a case report and literature review.. Frontiers in neuroscience 2026. doi:10.3389/fnins.2026.1859294. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Histopathological and immunohistochemical findings. Hematoxylin-eosin staining shows scattered spindle/stellate cells embedded in abundant myxoid stroma, consistent with myxoma morphology (a). Immunohistochemistry shows positivity for calretinin (b) and CD31 (c), and negativity for GFAP (d) and desmin (e). The morphology and immunophenotype support brain metastases from the previously resected atrial myxoma rather than a primary glial tumor or vascular malformation.
in_text_mentions: Postoperative histopathological examination revealed paucicellular myxoid neoplasms composed of scattered spindle or stellate cells with relatively abundant cytoplasm embedded in abundant myxoid stroma, with hemorrhagic change. These histological features closely resembled those of the previously resected atrial myxoma and supported extravascular tumor proliferation within the brain parenchyma (Figure 3a).

Immunohistochemical staining showed calretinin (+), CD31 (+), GFAP (–), and desmin (–) (Figures 3b–e). Calretinin positivity supported myxoma differentiation, CD31 positivity was compatible with a vascular-associated immunophenotype, GFAP negativity argued against a primary glial neoplasm, and desmin negativity argued against smooth or skeletal muscle differentiation.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A is an immunohistochemical (PD-L1, clone 22C3) stain of the surgically resected brain metastasis lesion, showing sheets of metastatic carcinoma cells with strong membranous PD-L1 positivity (CPS 98), confirming metastatic carcinoma in brain tissue. Article title and caption explicitly attribute the tissue to brain metastasis. B: Panel B is a second field (200x) of PD-L1 immunohistochemistry of the brain metastasis, showing diffuse membranous staining in tumor cells (TPS 95%), consistent with metastatic carcinoma in the brain. Caption and in-text mention explicitly link the specimen to the brain metastasis.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Axial CT from a case of sarcomatoid squamous cell carcinoma with brain metastases shows a large hyperdense falx-abutting mass with surrounding vasogenic edema. findings.label: Perilesional vasogenic edema
findings.evidence: subcortical roundish nodule located in the left frontal lobe, with low signal in T1WI ... surrounded by a large area of edema

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Axial non-contrast T1WI of a real patient showing a low-signal subcortical left frontal nodule with extensive surrounding edema, captioned as a suspicious metastatic lesion in a case report of brain metastases. B: Axial T2WI of the same patient demonstrating the metastatic nodule with concentric ring signal and extensive vasogenic edema, matching the captioned brain metastasis. C: Axial DWI of the same real patient; the captioned metastatic lesion shows no apparent diffusion restriction, a recognized (non-restricted) DWI appearance of brain metastases. The panel is part of the diagnostic characterization of the same lesion rather than a control image. D: Axial contrast-enhanced T1WI of a real patient showing a subcortical left frontal lesion with peripheral ring-like enhancement and extensive perilesional edema, captioned and described in text as an intracranial metastatic tumor.

in_text_mentions: gs was falsely attributed to the inability to penetrate through the BBB, which is composed of endothelial cells with tight junctions enwrapped with basement membrane, pericytes and astrocytes. However, tumor cells within the brain parenchyma release vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and other cytokines that increase vessel permeability [17,18]. Newer imaging techniques have proven that the BBB is dysfunctional in brain metastases as evidenced by leakage of contrast material into and around the tumors which basically rules out the BBB as the sole mechanism of drug resistance (Figure 2).

After 24 months post-diagnosis, recurrence was detected, including multiple brain metastases and lymph node metastases (Fig. 2). in_text_mentions: A 37-year-old female presented to the clinic in November 2014 with an unremitting upper respiratory tract infection. in_text_mentions: Three months after resuming enzalutamide, he began complaints of headaches. Brain CT revealed a single expansive left frontobasal lesion. At this time, both the PSA levels and thoraco-abdomino-pelvic CT remained stable (PSA of 2.91 ng/mL). A brain MRI was performed, which confirmed that it was a single lesion, measuring approximately 33 mm (Figure 2). After discussion in a Multidisciplinary Group with Neurosurgery and Radiation Oncology, surgery was scheduled. Given the epileptogenic potential of enzalutamide, it was again suspended at this time, maintaining goserelin (and atezolizumab).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Real patient MRI from a brain metastases case; caption identifies a dural-based tumor in the left parieto-occipital lobe, supporting dural/leptomeningeal involvement. Dural-based presentation is a less common form. B: Real patient MRI showing recurrent multiple brain lesions in a patient with known brain metastases; consistent with recurrent brain metastases. C: Real patient MRI from a brain metastases case showing progression of the major left parieto-occipital lesion, with surrounding FLAIR hyperintensity consistent with perilesional edema.

Eighteen months later, she presented with headache and diplopia, and received an MRI scan that showed a firm, dural-based tumor (7.0 cm × 5.0 cm) with hypervascularity in the left parieto-occipital lobe ( Figure 1A ). Tumor resection revealed pathology consistent with metastatic BC. She completed RT (40 Gy in 10 fractions) for the brain tumor bed and whole-brain RT (30 Gy in 10 fractions). In August 2020, she was given capecitabine, lapatinib, a GnRH agonist, and tamoxifen as first-line treatment for the metastatic BC.

A brain MRI scan in the following month showed recurrence, with multiple lesions in the left parieto-occipital region (largest: 3.4 cm × 2.9 cm × 4.1 cm) ( Figure 1B ). In March 2022, the patient received second-line treatment comprising capecitabine plus targeted therapy with neratinib, a GnRH agonist, and letrozole (her menses stopped in October 2021).
